All evidence converges on duodenal atresia as the single most likely structural etiology.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Bilateral bilious vomiting and feeding intolerance since birth — hallmark of high intestinal obstruction.  
- Abdominal ultrasound shows dilated fluid-filled proximal duodenum — consistent with proximal obstruction.  
- Upper GI series shows contrast abruptly terminating at the duodenal bulb with no passage distally — confirms complete obstruction at that level.  
- No pyloric hypertrophy on ultrasound — excludes hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.  
- Normal midgut rotation and preserved SMA/SVV relationship — excludes malrotation with volvulus.  
- No intrahepatic biliary dilation — argues against choledochal cyst or Alagille syndrome.  
- Electrolyte profile shows hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis — typical of chronic gastric acid loss from proximal obstruction/vomiting.  
- Clinical summary explicitly identifies duodenal atresia as the leading diagnosis supported by classic presentation and imaging.

[GAPS]  
- Meconium passage history is not specified — absence would support intrauterine obstruction onset (supporting atresia), but presence does not exclude it (some infants pass meconium before obstruction becomes clinically apparent).  
- Abdominal X-ray (“double-bubble” sign) is not described — though strongly implied by ultrasound and upper GI findings, direct confirmation would strengthen the diagnosis.  
- Karyotype result is pending — while trisomy 21 is a strong associative clue, its absence would not rule out duodenal atresia (most cases are sporadic), so this is supportive but not diagnostic.  
- Surgical or intraoperative findings are not available — definitive diagnosis requires histopathology or direct visualization, but imaging is >95% specific for atresia in this context.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Duodenal atresia
